effectsNote: Effects are added to the run when an option is chosen. months: development or launch delay; costUsd: extra cost; scienceDaysLost: days without observations; failureRiskPct: added chance of losing the mission; performancePct: change to the affected part's performance; sciencePct: change to the science score; dataBacklogDays: days of data waiting to be downlinked; propulsionUsePct: share of the propulsion capacity used; endsMission: the mission is lost.

events.name: Supplier delay
events.text: A supplier says one of your parts will arrive 4 months late.
events.why: Space parts are built in small numbers by a few companies. One missing component or a busy factory can hold up a whole project.
events.absorbedText: Your schedule had enough room, so the late part did not move the ready-for-launch date.

options.label: Buy a more expensive alternative part
options.outcome: You paid extra for a part from another supplier and kept the schedule.

options.label: Accept the delay
options.outcome: You waited 4 months for the part, and the team cost kept running.

events.name: Test failure
events.text: Your least mature part failed its vibration test.
events.why: Parts that have never flown (low TRL) have not yet proven they survive the shaking of launch and the vacuum of space. Ground tests find these problems before launch.
events.absorbedText: All your parts have flown before, so they passed their tests.

options.label: Fix and re-test the part
options.outcome: You fixed the part and it passed its second test, 3 months later.

options.label: Swap to a proven part
options.outcome: You swapped to a part that has flown before: safer, but less capable.

events.name: Launch delay
events.text: Bad weather and a rocket problem push the launch back by 1 month.
events.why: Rockets launch only when winds, clouds and every system are within safe limits. Rideshare satellites also wait for the main passenger to be ready.
events.absorbedText: Your mission was ready well before the deadline, so the delay did not matter.

options.label: Wait for the next attempt
options.outcome: The launch slipped by a month.

events.name: Launch failure
events.text: The rocket failed during ascent and the satellite was lost.
events.why: Every rocket has a track record. A launcher with fewer successful flights has a higher chance of failing, which is why cheap new rockets carry more risk.
events.absorbedText: The rocket worked and placed your satellite in orbit.

options.label: The mission ends
options.outcome: The satellite was lost at launch. The launcher's success rate decided this roll.

events.name: Solar storm
events.text: A strong solar storm is hitting Earth. Charged particles can upset the electronics.
events.why: The Sun sometimes throws out bursts of charged particles. They can flip bits in computers and damage parts that are not radiation-tolerant.
events.absorbedText: Your radiation-tolerant parts and power margin rode out the storm.

options.label: Enter safe mode
options.outcome: You entered safe mode and protected the satellite, losing 2 days of observations.

options.label: Keep operating
options.outcome: You kept observing through the storm and accepted the risk of damage.

events.name: Space debris approach
events.text: A piece of old rocket will pass very close to your satellite in 2 days.
events.why: Thousands of old satellites and fragments circle the Earth. Even a small piece hits hard at orbital speed, so operators move out of the way when they can.
events.absorbedText: The tracked debris passed at a safe distance.

options.label: Make an avoidance manoeuvre
options.outcome: You fired the thruster and moved out of the way, using some fuel.

options.label: Take the risk
options.outcome: You stayed on course and hoped the debris would miss.

events.name: Part failure
events.text: One of your parts has stopped working properly.
events.why: Parts wear out in space and cannot be repaired. Less mature parts fail more often, and a backup (redundancy) lets the mission continue.
events.absorbedText: Your parts are proven and kept working.

options.label: Switch to the backup
options.outcome: You switched to the backup and lost only a day of observations.

options.label: Continue degraded
options.outcome: The satellite kept working with reduced performance for the rest of the mission.

events.name: Ground station outage
events.text: One of your ground stations is down for a week after a storm damaged its antenna.
events.why: A satellite can only send data when it passes over a ground station. With fewer stations, data waits on board until the next contact.
events.absorbedText: Your other stations had enough spare contact time to carry the data.

options.label: Rent an extra station for a week
options.outcome: You rented time on another station and kept the data flowing.

options.label: Accept the data backlog
options.outcome: Data piled up on board and fire alerts arrived late for a week.

events.name: Major fire season
events.text: A hot, dry summer brings many fires. Firefighters ask for more observations.
events.why: This is what the mission was built for. More observations mean more data and more power, so spare capacity turns into extra science.
events.absorbedText: Your satellite had spare data and power capacity and delivered extra observations.

options.label: Increase observations
options.outcome: You observed more often and helped firefighters during the worst weeks.

options.label: Keep the normal plan
options.outcome: You kept the normal observation plan and missed some of the fires.

sources.note: Effect sizes and draw weights are starting values for balancing.
